sections.markdown:
## C2 — Night driving, defensive observation and sight distance

FACT_ID: sec15-R01 | anchor: A02
With good tires and brakes on dry pavement, the handbook estimates that reacting and stopping from 50 mph can require about 400 feet. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec15-R02 | anchor: A02
Under the stated good-tire, good-brake and dry-pavement conditions, the handbook gives about 200 feet as a stopping example at 30 mph. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec15-R03 | anchor: A02
If sight distance is below the stopping example for a given speed, there may be insufficient time to avoid an object once it becomes visible. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec15-R04 | anchor: A02
At night, travel slowly enough to stop within the distance illuminated by the headlights. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec15-R05 | anchor: A02
The handbook says visibility limited to about 200 feet or less in heavy rain, snow or fog does not support speeds above 30 mph. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec15-R06 | anchor: A02
If rain becomes too heavy to see well enough to drive, pull off in a safe place and wait for it to clear. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec15-R07 | anchor: A02
Slow for a hill or curve that hides the roadway so a stop remains possible for an unseen obstruction. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec15-R08 | anchor: A03
Give parked vehicles as much safe clearance as possible because they obscure people exiting or walking between them. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec15-R09 | anchor: A03
The four-second sight-distance rule checks whether vehicle speed is too high for how far ahead the driver can see. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec15-R10 | anchor: A03
Choose a stationary object at the farthest clearly visible point and count four seconds while approaching it. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec15-R11 | anchor: A03
If you reach the sight-distance marker before four seconds have elapsed, slow down because speed is too high for the visible distance. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec15-R12 | anchor: A03
Use the four-second sight-distance check at night to avoid outdriving the headlights. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec15-R13 | anchor: A03
Obey speed limits because they reflect road design, vehicle use and hidden entry points as well as traffic volume. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec15-R14 | anchor: A03
Posted limits assume ideal conditions; wet or icy pavement, poor vision or heavy traffic can require a lower speed. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec15-R15 | anchor: A03
A driver can be ticketed for speed that is unsafe for conditions even while below the posted limit. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec15-R16 | anchor: A03
Maintaining space around the vehicle creates a time cushion for reacting to other road users. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec15-R17 | anchor: A03
The three-second rule is introduced as a way to judge following distance, distinct from the four-second sight-distance check. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0127]
